opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing that excites me is that we've never really had a way to run experiments on whole societies. Economics and sociology are mostly stuck with observational data, plus a handful of natural experiments. If you want to know what happens to a town when most of the jobs get automated, or when people start getting most of their information from a single AI assistant, you basically have to wait for it to happen and then argue about it afterwards.

With LLM agents you can at least sketch a version of that. You set up a little village of a few dozen or a few hundred agents, give them roles, needs, some resources, a way to trade and talk to each other, and then you change something and watch what follows. Does trust break down? Do people form coalitions? Does some kind of norm emerge on its own? It's crude, but it's a sandbox where you can rerun history with different parameters, which no one has ever been able to do with actual humans.

The part I care about most, given my worries about gradual disempowerment, is that a lot of the dynamics I'm concerned about are emergent and slow. No single decision looks bad. It's more like each firm or each government individually finds it a bit more efficient to rely on AI and a bit less necessary to keep humans in the loop, and over time human leverage just quietly erodes. That's very hard to reason about from the armchair, and it's exactly the kind of thing where a simulation, even an imperfect one, could make the intuition more concrete. You might actually see the moment where the humans in the village stop mattering to how resources get allocated.

I want to be honest about the limitations, though. These agents aren't people. They're often too agreeable and too homogeneous, and they reflect whatever the model was trained to sound like. So I wouldn't take any particular number out of these simulations very seriously. I think of them more as tools for generating hypotheses and stress-testing stories. If someone says "markets will obviously keep humans relevant" or "democracy will obviously correct for this," you can at least build a toy world and check whether that story holds up even in the toy case. If it fails there, that tells you something.

And over time, as the models get better at modeling real human behavior, these could become genuinely useful for policy, something like a wind tunnel for institutions. You could try out a new voting mechanism or a UBI scheme or an AI governance regime in simulation before deploying it on real people. We're not there yet, but I think it's one of the more underexplored directions.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents with roles, needs, resources, and trade, but does not say these simulations model economic activity at finer detail than conventional economic models.

r002.rationale: It mentions watching whether norms emerge, but does not connect the simulations to identifying the drivers of cultural evolution.

r003.rationale: It mentions trust, coalitions, democracy, and governance, but does not say the simulations could identify conditions for political stability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that excites me most is that for a long time, the questions I actually care about — what happens to a society when you change its incentives, or when a bunch of agents can delegate their decisions, or when some group gets gradually disempowered — were basically off-limits to experiment. You can't run a controlled trial on a country. You can build an agent-based model with little rules-following dots, but those dots don't understand anything. They don't have goals in any rich sense, they can't negotiate, they can't notice that the rules have changed and route around them. So the models were always a bit of a cartoon, and the people who built them knew that.

What's changed is that now you can populate those models with agents that are, let's say, a cheap approximation of a person. They can read a contract, haggle, form a plan, gossip about each other, decide to cooperate or defect for reasons they can articulate. And once you have that, a lot of questions in economics and political theory that were only ever argued about verbally become something you can at least poke at empirically. You can ask: if I give everyone in this village an AI assistant that's slightly better at their job than they are, what happens to who ends up owning what? Does the whole thing drift toward a few actors controlling everything, or does it stay pluralistic? What institutions survive? And you can re-run it a thousand times with different parameters instead of waiting for history to give you one noisy sample.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I think the failure mode is obvious. These simulated agents are not people. They've got whatever quirks the base model has, they're probably more agreeable and more homogeneous than real humans, and it would be very easy to get a result that's an artifact of the model's training rather than a fact about social dynamics. So I don't think of these as predictions. I think of them more like a flight simulator for intuitions. They can tell you "here's a mechanism that could happen," and then you go check it against the real world or against theory.

And honestly, the thing I'm most interested in using them for is the gradual disempowerment stuff. The worry there isn't a dramatic takeover, it's a slow shift where humans become economically and politically irrelevant because machines do everything better and the systems that used to need us stop needing us. That's exactly the kind of slow, multi-agent, incentive-driven process that's hard to reason about on a whiteboard and that you'd never want to learn about by living through it. If a miniature economy can show us the early warning signs of that transition — what it looks like when a system quietly stops being accountable to the people inside it — that seems genuinely valuable, even if the little villages are crude.

r001.rationale: It contrasts simplistic rule-following agents with richer agents that can negotiate, plan, and respond to changed rules, then describes probing economic questions in a miniature economy. This communicates modeling economic activity in greater detail than conventional agent-based models.

r002.rationale: The response mentions agents gossiping, but it does not suggest using simulations to identify drivers of cultural evolution.

r003.rationale: It asks what institutions survive and whether control remains pluralistic, but does not clearly frame the simulations as identifying conditions for political stability.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is that you can start to study situations where the interesting behaviour comes from interactions between people. You could give agents different information, different incentives, and different opportunities to communicate, and then ask: do they manage to coordinate? Does a rumour spread? Does some institution help them cooperate?

The exciting part is that you can intervene. You can run the same little economy with a different rule, or change who knows what, and see what happens. That gives you a way to explore mechanisms that might be quite hard to isolate in the real world.

But there’s a big gap between producing a plausible-looking village and producing a useful model of human behaviour. All your villagers might share the same underlying model and the same biases. And they might act out a familiar story about how an economy works, rather than respond in the way actual people would.

So I’d be excited about using these simulations to generate hypotheses, and then checking those hypotheses against observations or experiments. The fact that the agents can give you a convincing explanation of what they’re doing doesn’t, by itself, mean the simulation is telling you something true.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling interactions and interventions in a miniature economy, but does not compare its level of detail with conventional economic models.

r002.rationale: It mentions coordination, rumors, and cooperation, but does not suggest using simulations to identify drivers of cultural evolution.

r003.rationale: It mentions institutions that might help people cooperate, but does not suggest identifying conditions for political stability.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is that you can start to model situations where the details of how people think and communicate actually matter. In a simple economic model, you might assume that everyone is perfectly rational, or give each agent a few rules. With language models, you can give agents different information and incentives, and let them negotiate, make plans, or misunderstand each other.

Then you can ask questions like: Does cooperation emerge? What happens when you change the rules? Can one agent manipulate the others? You have a little laboratory where you can inspect what happened and run the experiment again.

The big caveat is that a convincing simulation isn’t necessarily an accurate one. These agents might share biases or behave similarly because they’re all instances of the same model. So I’m more excited about using this to generate hypotheses and study interactions between AI agents than assuming we’ve suddenly got a reliable simulator of human society.

r001.rationale: It says LLM agents can model details of how people think and communicate, unlike conventional models that assume perfect rationality or use a few rules.

r002.rationale: It discusses studying cooperation and agent interactions, but does not suggest identifying drivers of cultural evolution.

r003.rationale: It does not mention political stability or conditions that produce it.
